$schemaNote: Draft content for There and Back — Journey catalog. NOT final: map.json pixel coordinates, l10n keys and human narrative polish still pending. See CLAUDE.md §4/§6.2 for target schema. `narrative` is the in-fiction traveler's line (what the app shows); `historicalNote`, present on about half the landmarks, is a short real-world historical/archaeological aside (not shown to the traveler as-is — candidate copy for a future 'about this place' surface) and is added only where a genuine, checkable anchor exists, not on every point. Each segment also carries `departureHour` (0-24, the in-fiction local hour at `fromMeters`) and `durationDays` (in-fiction days elapsed crossing to `toMeters`) — CLAUDE.md §6.1's fictional sky reads these, via `fictionalHourFor`, to show the story's own time of day at the route position the 'Путь' scene is scrolled to. `durationDays` is capped by a pace-safety rule (`journey_timing_repository.dart`): at most 1 in-fiction day per 10 000 real meters of the segment, so an ordinary walk can never flip the sky through several story-days at once — several episodes below (month/year/multi-year mythic stays) are deliberately compressed well under their literal duration for this reason, noted in `timeNote`. `timeNote`, like `historicalNote`, is added only where a genuine textual anchor exists.

journey.name: The Odyssey: Troy to Ithaca
journey.source: Homer's Odyssey — public domain (composed c. 8th century BCE; not protected by copyright or trademark anywhere)

segments.name: Troy — The Departure
segments.timeNote: Homer's recurring departure formula — 'rosy-fingered Dawn appeared'

segments.name: The Storm off Cape Malea
segments.timeNote: Text: 'nine days was I driven by fell winds'; reduced to 6 to stay under this segment's pace-safety cap

segments.name: Aeolia — Isle of the Winds
segments.timeNote: Text: 'a whole month he entertained me' plus a failed return voyage; compressed well below the literal weeks under the pace-safety cap

segments.name: The Laestrygonian Fjord
segments.timeNote: Text: 'for seven days...till on the eighth we reached...the Laestrygonian city'

segments.name: Aeaea — Circe's Isle (First Stay)
segments.timeNote: Text: 'you are already a full year here' — compressed well below the literal year under the pace-safety cap

segments.name: The Shore of the Dead
segments.timeNote: Land of the Cimmerians, 'the sun never looks on them with his rays' — kept within the night/dusk bands on purpose

segments.name: The Strait of Scylla and Charybdis
Thrinacia — Pastures of the Sun
segments.timeNote: Text: 'for a whole month the South wind blew' becalmed — compressed well below the literal month under the pace-safety cap

segments.name: Adrift Alone
segments.timeNote: Text: 'nine days I was carried this way and that...in the night of the tenth' reaches Ogygia; reduced to 7 for margin under this segment's pace-safety cap

segments.name: Ogygia — Calypso's Isle
segments.timeNote: Text: kept there 'seven years' — the longest of this quest's compressed stays, deliberately capped at 7 in-fiction days rather than 2555

segments.name: The Raft and Poseidon's Storm
segments.timeNote: Text: about seventeen days' calm sail then Poseidon's storm; compressed under the pace-safety cap

segments.name: The Night Passage Home
segments.timeNote: Text: a single overnight voyage on the magic Phaeacian ship

segments.name: Ithaca — The Homecoming
segments.timeNote: Recognition, the bow contest and the reckoning span roughly 40 narrated days; compressed under the pace-safety cap

landmarks.name: The Smoking Walls of Troy
landmarks.narrative: Smoke still curls above the broken towers as the ships push off.
landmarks.historicalNote: Troy is usually identified with the archaeological mound of Hisarlik in northwestern Turkey; Heinrich Schliemann's 1870s excavations there uncovered several destruction layers, one of them (Troy VIIa) burned around 1180 BCE — in the rough era later Greeks assigned to the Trojan War.

landmarks.name: The Harbor of a Thousand Ships
landmarks.narrative: Counted the empty berths where the fleet once rode at anchor.
landmarks.historicalNote: The Iliad's 'Catalogue of Ships' lists forces from across the Greek world; ancient audiences already treated its huge fleet count as a feat of oral memory rather than a literal muster roll.

landmarks.name: The Last Sight of the Trojan Shore
landmarks.narrative: Watched the coastline shrink to a grey line on the horizon.
landmarks.historicalNote: Ancient Aegean sailors mostly hugged the coast rather than crossing open water; losing sight of land was itself considered a notable, risky moment worth marking in the story.

landmarks.name: The Walls of Ismarus
landmarks.narrative: Raided the granaries before the Cicones could raise the alarm.
landmarks.historicalNote: The Cicones were a real Thracian people, also named among Troy's allies in the Iliad; ancient geographers placed them on the Thracian coast near the river Hebrus (today's Maritsa).

landmarks.name: The Vineyard Slopes Above the Town
landmarks.narrative: Filled the water-skins with dark wine taken from the hillside.
landmarks.historicalNote: Wine from Ismarus/Maroneia was famous in antiquity for its strength — the very wine Odysseus later uses to get the Cyclops drunk.

landmarks.name: The Cicones' Muster Field
landmarks.narrative: Watched dust rise on the inland road — reinforcements are coming.

landmarks.name: The Retreat to the Ships
landmarks.narrative: Fought a rearguard action back across the open beach.

landmarks.name: The Bloodied Sands of Ismarus
landmarks.narrative: Counted six men lost from every ship before the last oar bit water.
landmarks.historicalNote: The poem gives an unusually exact casualty figure here — six men lost per ship — a precision that stands out against the vaguer numbers used almost everywhere else in the epic.

landmarks.name: The Turn at Cape Malea
landmarks.narrative: The current seized the ships the moment we rounded the cape.
landmarks.historicalNote: Cape Malea, the Peloponnese's southern tip, had a real reputation among ancient Greek sailors as the most dangerous headland to round; a saying quoted by the geographer Strabo warns to 'forget everything at home' once past it.

landmarks.name: Nine Days Before the North Wind
landmarks.narrative: Lost all sense of east and west under the driving gale.

landmarks.name: The Uncharted Swell
landmarks.narrative: The known sea-lanes are gone; nothing ahead looks familiar.
landmarks.historicalNote: From here the poem's geography stops matching any real Mediterranean coastline — ancient and modern scholars alike treat everything past Malea as folklore, not itinerary.

landmarks.name: The Lotus-Eaters' Shore
landmarks.narrative: A strange sweetness hangs in the air the moment we land.
landmarks.historicalNote: The historian Herodotus describes a real people he calls the Lotophagi living on the Libyan coast (roughly modern Tunisia), eating a sweet fruit-bread — the episode's closest widely cited real-world anchor.

landmarks.name: The Grove of the Honeyed Fruit
landmarks.narrative: Three scouts sent inland; only two remember why they came.

landmarks.name: Dragging the Dreamers Back
landmarks.narrative: Bound a lotus-eater to his bench to keep him from the shore.

landmarks.name: Rowing Away From Forgetting
landmarks.narrative: Pulled hard for open water before the sweetness took the rest of us.

landmarks.name: The Goat Island Offshore
landmarks.narrative: Anchored on the small island across from the cave-dweller's coast.
landmarks.historicalNote: Ancient writers as early as Thucydides associated the Cyclopes with Sicily, whose volcanic landscape gave later audiences a ready image for a one-eyed, fire-breathing race.

landmarks.name: The Cliffside Cave Mouth
landmarks.narrative: A cave big enough for a giant's flock, sealed with a single boulder.
landmarks.historicalNote: The blinded-giant-in-a-cave story is catalogued by folklorists as an old, widespread tale type found well beyond Greece — Homer appears to be adapting existing oral tradition, not inventing it.

landmarks.name: The Cheese-Racks in the Dark
landmarks.narrative: Found the shelves stacked with cheeses and pens crowded with lambs.

landmarks.name: Polyphemus's Hearthstone
landmarks.narrative: The giant returned and rolled a stone no ten men could move.
landmarks.historicalNote: 'Cyclopean masonry' is a real archaeological term for the massive, irregular stone walls at Mycenae and Tiryns — later Greeks found them so large they assumed only the Cyclopes could have built them.

landmarks.name: The Sharpened Olive Stake
landmarks.narrative: Hardened the point in the embers while the giant slept off the wine.

landmarks.name: The Blinding of the Cyclops
landmarks.narrative: Drove the stake home; his roar shook dust from the cave roof.

landmarks.name: Beneath the Rams' Bellies
landmarks.narrative: Lashed under the fleece of the biggest rams to slip past his groping hands.

landmarks.name: The Boulder-Throw Shallows
landmarks.narrative: Torn rock splashed close enough to swamp the stern.
landmarks.historicalNote: Real volcanic rock formations off the Sicilian coast near Aci Trezza — the 'Faraglioni dei Ciclopi' — were identified by later folk tradition as the very stones Polyphemus hurled.

landmarks.name: Shouting a Name Across the Water
landmarks.narrative: A boast thrown back at the shore that we may come to regret.
landmarks.historicalNote: Withholding one's true name from an enemy is a widespread folklore taboo; Odysseus breaking it here to boast is read by scholars as the hinge that turns a lucky escape into a twenty-year punishment.

landmarks.name: Clear of the Cyclops' Coast
landmarks.narrative: Rowed until the giant's cries were just an echo on the wind.

landmarks.name: The Floating Walls of Aeolia
landmarks.narrative: An island ringed by unbroken bronze, adrift on a sea of its own.
landmarks.historicalNote: The Lipari Islands north of Sicily are still called the Aeolian Islands today, the ancient identification of Aeolus's floating home.

landmarks.name: The Hall of the Wind-King
landmarks.narrative: Feasted a full month as guest of the keeper of the winds.

landmarks.name: The Ox-Hide Sack of Storms
landmarks.narrative: Given every contrary wind bound tight in a sack of ox-hide.
landmarks.historicalNote: Winds bound inside a container is a recognized motif in sailors' folklore across many maritime cultures, not a detail unique to this poem.

landmarks.name: Sighting Ithaca's Smoke
landmarks.narrative: Home fires were visible on the horizon before curiosity ruined it.

landmarks.name: The Sack Torn Open by Greed
landmarks.narrative: The crew loosed the bindings, certain it held hidden gold.

landmarks.name: Blown Back to Where We Started
landmarks.narrative: Every mile of the voyage undone in a single gale.

landmarks.name: The Narrow Fjord Harbor
landmarks.narrative: Steep cliffs on both sides, water too still to trust.
landmarks.historicalNote: The unusually short summer nights described here have led some scholars to read this episode as a garbled sailor's account of high-latitude northern seas, where midsummer nights are genuinely brief.

landmarks.name: The Giant Queen's Doorway
landmarks.narrative: Sent scouts to the king's hall; only the horror of it returned.

landmarks.name: The Boulders From the Cliffs Above
landmarks.narrative: Rocks the size of ships crashed down on the fleet at anchor.
landmarks.historicalNote: Only one of twelve ships survives this attack — the single largest loss of the whole voyage, after which Odysseus sails on with just his own crew.

landmarks.name: The Speared Catch
landmarks.narrative: Watched crewmen gathered up on giant spears like fish on a line.

landmarks.name: The One Ship That Cleared the Strait
landmarks.narrative: Cut the mooring line rather than wait for the tide.

landmarks.name: Counting What the Fjord Took
landmarks.narrative: Eleven ships lost in the time it takes to draw one breath.

landmarks.name: The Smoke Above Aeaea
landmarks.narrative: A single thread of hearth-smoke rising from an island of dense oak.
landmarks.historicalNote: Ancient geographers as far back as the Roman period identified Aeaea with the Monte Circeo promontory on the Italian coast — in some reconstructions of past sea levels, genuinely once an island.

landmarks.name: The Wolves That Do Not Bite
landmarks.narrative: Lions and wolves circled the scouting party like tame hounds.

landmarks.name: Circe's Loom Song
landmarks.narrative: Heard weaving and singing through the open doorway of a fine house.
landmarks.historicalNote: Weaving was the archetypal domestic craft of the Greek household; showing Circe at the loom quietly links her, visually, to Penelope waiting at her own loom back in Ithaca.

landmarks.name: The Cup of Forgetting
landmarks.narrative: Watched half the crew take the offered wine without a second thought.

landmarks.name: The Sty Behind the House
landmarks.narrative: Found the missing men penned as swine, still weeping with human eyes.

landmarks.name: The Moly Root at the Crossroads
landmarks.narrative: A grey-and-white herb, pressed into hand, said to turn a curse aside.
landmarks.historicalNote: The 'moly' herb Odysseus is given — black root, white flower — has never been matched to a real plant despite the unusually precise botanical description, and scholars still argue over what Homer had in mind.

landmarks.name: The Untouched Cup
landmarks.narrative: Drank the wine and did not fall; the witch's spell had no purchase.

landmarks.name: The Bargain on Circe's Threshold
landmarks.narrative: A blade at her throat bought a year's welcome instead of a curse.

landmarks.name: The Swine Restored to Men
landmarks.narrative: Watched bristles fall away and old faces return, more grieved than glad.

landmarks.name: A Year at Aeaea's Table
landmarks.narrative: Twelve months of feasting while the ships sit idle on the sand.
landmarks.historicalNote: A full year at Circe's table is the second-longest single stop of the whole journey, behind only Calypso's island.

landmarks.name: The Edge of Ocean's Stream
landmarks.narrative: Sailed past the sunless edge of the world into fog that never lifts.
landmarks.historicalNote: Archaic Greeks pictured the inhabited world as a flat disk ringed by a great river-Ocean; setting the entrance to the dead at its edge follows that real cosmology directly.

landmarks.name: The Grove of Persephone
landmarks.narrative: Black poplars and dead willows mark the entrance to the House of the Dead.
landmarks.historicalNote: Some ancient sources placed this land of the dead near Ephyra in northwestern Greece, where a real 'Nekyomanteion' — an oracle for consulting the dead — once operated; later excavators' identification of the exact site has since been disputed.

landmarks.name: The Trench of Dark Blood
landmarks.narrative: Dug a pit and filled it with offerings to call the shades to speech.
landmarks.historicalNote: Pouring blood into a pit to draw and question the dead reflects a genuine ancient Greek necromantic rite, attested independently at real oracle-of-the-dead sites.

landmarks.name: The Shade of Elpenor, Unburied
landmarks.narrative: A crewman's ghost begs for a grave he does not yet know he needs.
landmarks.historicalNote: Proper burial mattered enormously in ancient Greek religion — Elpenor's plea for a grave voices a real and deeply held belief, not just a plot device.

landmarks.name: The Blind Prophet's Warning
landmarks.narrative: Tiresias speaks of a homecoming bought at the price of every companion.
landmarks.historicalNote: Tiresias, the blind prophet of Thebes, is a major figure across Greek myth far beyond the Odyssey — most famously in the later story of Oedipus.

landmarks.name: My Mother's Shade Among the Dead
landmarks.narrative: Reached three times to embrace her; three times the shade slipped through.
landmarks.historicalNote: The failed embrace of a parent's ghost here is echoed almost word for word later in the poem, when Odysseus embraces his very-much-alive father Laertes.

landmarks.name: The Judgment Hall of Minos
landmarks.narrative: Watched the dead lining up for a verdict none of the living can hear.

landmarks.name: Orion's Endless Hunt
landmarks.narrative: A hunter's shade still drives ghostly beasts across the asphodel field.

landmarks.name: The Weight Sisyphus Cannot Set Down
landmarks.narrative: A boulder, a slope, and a curse with no end in sight.
landmarks.historicalNote: Sisyphus's pointless, endless labor became so proverbial that 'Sisyphean' is still ordinary English for futile toil, three thousand years later.

landmarks.name: The Retreat From the House of the Dead
landmarks.narrative: Ran for the ship before the countless dead pressed too close.

landmarks.name: Elpenor's Barrow on the Shore
landmarks.narrative: Raised a mound and planted an oar where the fallen crewman rests.
landmarks.historicalNote: Marking a lost sailor's grave with a planted oar reflects a real ancient Greek custom of symbolic burial markers for those lost far from home.

landmarks.name: Circe's Chart of Dangers Ahead
landmarks.narrative: Warned in careful detail of every horror still waiting on the route home.

landmarks.name: The Wax and the Mast Ropes
landmarks.narrative: Prepared beeswax for the ears and rope enough to bind a man fast.
landmarks.historicalNote: Beeswax was an ordinary, widely available ancient Mediterranean material — one of the epic's most famous solutions is also one of its most mundane.

landmarks.name: The Becalmed Approach to the Sirens
landmarks.narrative: Not a breath of wind stirs as the fatal coast comes into view.
landmarks.historicalNote: Ancient tradition placed the Sirens' rocks off the Sorrentine peninsula in Italy, on a cluster of islets still known today as Li Galli — once called the Sirenusae.

landmarks.name: Ears Sealed With Wax
landmarks.narrative: Watched the rowers' faces go blank and calm as the wax set.
landmarks.historicalNote: Early Greek art shows the Sirens as bird-bodied women, not the fish-tailed figure later cultures came to call a 'siren'.

landmarks.name: Bound to the Mast
landmarks.narrative: Lashed tight at my own order, straining against ropes I begged for.
landmarks.historicalNote: This scene — the one sailor who heard the Sirens and lived, bound to his own mast — became one of antiquity's most painted images, appearing on Greek vases for centuries.

landmarks.name: The Field of Bones Below the Rocks
landmarks.narrative: White bones catch the light on the meadow beneath the singing cliff.

landmarks.name: The Smoking Whirlpool
landmarks.narrative: Charybdis swallows the sea itself three times a day.
landmarks.historicalNote: The historian Thucydides already identified this strait with the real Strait of Messina between Sicily and mainland Italy, genuinely known for strong tidal currents.

landmarks.name: The Cliff With No Handhold
landmarks.narrative: A sheer rock face, and somewhere in its caves, six mouths waiting.

landmarks.name: The Choice of Losses
landmarks.narrative: Steer wide of the whirlpool and pay the narrow strait its price instead.
landmarks.historicalNote: 'Between Scylla and Charybdis' survives today, in English and other languages, as an idiom for choosing between two comparably bad options.

landmarks.name: Scylla's Reach
landmarks.narrative: Six men snatched from the deck before the ship had fully passed.

landmarks.name: Their Cries Above the Water
landmarks.narrative: Called my name as the current pulled the ship onward, out of reach.

landmarks.name: Clear Water Past the Narrows
landmarks.narrative: The strait widens; the screaming fades faster than it should.

landmarks.name: The Sun God's Green Island
landmarks.narrative: Cattle graze in herds too perfect to be ordinary livestock.
landmarks.historicalNote: Thrinacia's name echoes an old Greek epithet for Sicily itself, 'Trinacria' — 'three-cornered,' describing the island's triangular shape.

landmarks.name: The Oath Sworn on the Beach
landmarks.narrative: Every man swears not to touch a single one of the sacred herd.

landmarks.name: A Month Pinned by Contrary Winds
landmarks.narrative: No wind fit for sailing; the stores run thinner every day.

landmarks.name: The Last of the Ship's Bread
landmarks.narrative: Hunger starts to argue louder than any oath sworn on a beach.

landmarks.name: The Slaughter of the Sacred Cattle
landmarks.narrative: Smoke from a forbidden fire rises while I sleep on the headland.

landmarks.name: The Hides That Crawled at Night
landmarks.narrative: Flayed skins seen moving, and the roasting meat groaning like a living thing.

landmarks.name: A Clear Sky That Brings No Comfort
landmarks.narrative: The wind finally turns fair — too late to undo what was eaten.

landmarks.name: The Lightning Bolt Offshore
landmarks.narrative: Zeus splits the mast the moment the ship clears the sacred coast.

landmarks.name: The Wreck Where the Crew Was Lost
landmarks.narrative: Every companion gone in a single strike; only planking remains.

landmarks.name: Riding the Mast Alone
landmarks.narrative: Lashed keel to broken mast and let the current choose the course.

landmarks.name: Back Through Charybdis, Somehow
landmarks.narrative: The same whirlpool that ate a fleet spares one man clinging to driftwood.

landmarks.name: Nine Days on Open Water
landmarks.narrative: No land, no ship, no crew — just current and a fig tree remembered too well.
landmarks.historicalNote: The number nine recurs through the poem at oddly regular intervals — nine days of storm earlier, nine days adrift here — a pattern 20th-century scholarship on oral-formulaic composition (Milman Parry) traces to the mechanics of composing epic aloud, not coincidence.

landmarks.name: Washed Up on Ogygia's Sand
landmarks.narrative: A nymph's hidden island, further from home than any place yet.
landmarks.historicalNote: Ogygia's location was disputed even in antiquity, with ancient writers proposing sites from Malta and Gozo to the far Atlantic; most modern scholars treat it as deliberately unmappable rather than a real island.

landmarks.name: Calypso's Grotto Fire
landmarks.narrative: Cedar and citrus smoke drift from a cave mouth wreathed in vines.

landmarks.name: The Offer of Forever
landmarks.narrative: Immortality offered in exchange for never seeing Ithaca again.
landmarks.historicalNote: Calypso's offer of immortality, and Odysseus's refusal of it, is read by many scholars as the poem's clearest statement of its actual theme — choosing a mortal home over a god's endless, changeless life.

landmarks.name: The Loom by the Cave Entrance
landmarks.narrative: Days measured out in weaving, waiting, and watching an empty horizon.

landmarks.name: Seven Years Counted in Tides
landmarks.narrative: The seasons on Ogygia repeat with no calendar but the surf.
landmarks.historicalNote: Seven years on Ogygia is the single longest stop of the entire twenty-year absence from Ithaca — more than double any other stay in the poem.

landmarks.name: Hermes on the Sea-Bright Path
landmarks.narrative: A messenger sandaled in wind arrives at Calypso's door, unannounced.

landmarks.name: The Order From Olympus
landmarks.narrative: Reluctantly, the nymph agrees to let her guest build a raft and leave.

landmarks.name: Felling Timber for the Raft
landmarks.narrative: Twenty trees cut, trimmed, and lashed with the last tools she'll lend.
landmarks.historicalNote: The mortise-and-tenon joinery real Bronze Age shipbuilders used is confirmed by actual shipwrecks, such as the Uluburun wreck recovered off the Turkish coast.

landmarks.name: Eighteen Days by the Stars
landmarks.narrative: Kept the Great Bear on the left hand, exactly as instructed.
landmarks.historicalNote: Keeping a fixed constellation — here the Great Bear — on one side of the vessel was a real, attested method of ancient celestial navigation, not a poetic flourish.

landmarks.name: Poseidon's Sighting From Afar
landmarks.narrative: A god still furious over a blinded son notices the raft too late to ignore.
landmarks.historicalNote: Poseidon's grudge over his blinded son is the epic's own explicitly stated reason for the entire twenty-year ordeal — one of Greek myth's most clearly drawn cause-and-effect stories of divine anger.

landmarks.name: The Wave That Broke the Mast
landmarks.narrative: One strike from the sea-god's trident undoes eighteen days of careful sailing.

landmarks.name: Clinging to a Single Plank
landmarks.narrative: Ino's veil, tied at the waist, is the only thing between here and drowning.
landmarks.historicalNote: Ino, the sea-goddess who intervenes here, was a mortal woman in other tellings of Greek myth before her transformation — one of several such divinized former mortals in Greek religion.

landmarks.name: The River Mouth of Salvation
landmarks.narrative: A gentle current, unlike any other on this voyage, finally welcomes rather than fights.

landmarks.name: Sleeping in a Bed of Leaves
landmarks.narrative: Two olive trees grown together make the first safe shelter in weeks.

landmarks.name: Nausicaa's Washing Day
landmarks.narrative: A princess and her maids find a castaway asleep among the driftwood.
landmarks.historicalNote: A princess doing the household's laundry herself, rather than leaving it to servants, is a small realistic detail scholars read as marking Phaeacian society as idealized and unusually unpretentious.

landmarks.name: The Gift of Oil and Linen
landmarks.narrative: Clean clothes and oil for aching limbs, offered without a single question.
landmarks.historicalNote: Bathing with oil rather than soap was standard ancient Mediterranean hygiene — the gift here is thoroughly ordinary, not exotic.

landmarks.name: The Road Into the Phaeacian City
landmarks.narrative: Advised to enter alone and unnoticed, and to beg the queen, not the king.

landmarks.name: Athena's Mist Along the Streets
landmarks.narrative: Walked through the market unseen, cloaked in a goddess's favor.

landmarks.name: The Queen's Hearth
landmarks.narrative: Knelt at Arete's feet before a single word of welcome was offered.
landmarks.historicalNote: Ancient commentators already noted that a supplicant here approaches the queen, not the king — an unusual detail suggesting real authority for Phaeacian queens.

landmarks.name: The Feast in King Alcinous's Hall
landmarks.narrative: Bread, wine, and a full accounting of the story so far, demanded by curious hosts.

landmarks.name: The Blind Singer's Song of Troy
landmarks.narrative: A bard sings the fall of Troy, and the guest weeps without meaning to.
landmarks.historicalNote: The blind court singer Demodocus is often read as Homer's own self-portrait, since later ancient biography also imagined Homer himself as blind.

landmarks.name: The Games on the Practice Field
landmarks.narrative: A discus throw settles an insult before it becomes a feud.
landmarks.historicalNote: Athletic contests as a mark of hospitality reflect the same competitive culture that, in the real world, produced institutions like the ancient Olympic Games.

landmarks.name: Demodocus Sings the Wooden Horse
landmarks.narrative: The whole hall falls silent at the story only one listener truly lived.
landmarks.historicalNote: The Trojan Horse is never narrated in the Iliad itself — this scene, sung by Demodocus, is actually the earliest surviving account of it, making the Odyssey older than the Iliad on that one detail.

landmarks.name: Naming the Castaway at Last
landmarks.narrative: After days of silence, the guest finally gives his name to the hall.

landmarks.name: The Magic Ship Made Ready
landmarks.narrative: A Phaeacian galley loaded with gifts greater than anything brought from Troy.
landmarks.historicalNote: Phaeacian ships needing no steering, described here as almost magically fast, are punished later in the same book — turned to stone by Poseidon on their way home, a fate the poem recounts right after Odysseus's own safe arrival.

landmarks.name: Asleep for the Last Crossing
landmarks.narrative: Slept through the whole voyage; the ship needs no hand on the oar.

landmarks.name: Waking on an Unfamiliar Shore
landmarks.narrative: Twenty years gone; even home looks like a stranger's coastline.
landmarks.historicalNote: Ithaca's exact identity among the Ionian Islands has been argued since antiquity; a modern theory (Robert Bittlestone, 2005) proposed the Paliki peninsula of Cephalonia as the 'real' Ithaca, though most scholars still favor the traditionally named island, Ithaki.

landmarks.name: The Harbor of the Old Sea-God Phorcys
landmarks.narrative: A hidden cove ringed with olive trees, exactly as the stories described it.

landmarks.name: The Cave of the Nymphs
landmarks.narrative: Stone looms and stone jars inside a cave no mortal built.
landmarks.historicalNote: A real cave near Polis Bay on modern Ithaki has long been proposed as this 'Cave of the Nymphs,' partly on the strength of ancient votive offerings archaeologists found there.

landmarks.name: Athena's Disguise on the Beach
landmarks.narrative: Advice from a shepherd who is clearly no shepherd at all.

landmarks.name: Hiding the Phaeacian Gold
landmarks.narrative: Treasure buried in the cave before a single step is taken inland.

landmarks.name: The Swineherd's Hut on the Ridge
landmarks.narrative: Smoke rising from Eumaeus's hut, the first honest welcome in twenty years.
landmarks.historicalNote: Eumaeus the swineherd is one of the few enslaved or low-status characters in Homeric epic given real depth and a voice of his own — a detail scholars single out as unusual for the genre.

landmarks.name: A Beggar at His Own Door
landmarks.narrative: Disguised past recognition, even by the dogs that once knew him.

landmarks.name: The Old Dog on the Dung Heap
landmarks.narrative: Argos lifts his head once, at a scent no one else in the yard notices.
landmarks.historicalNote: The old dog Argos recognizing his master and then dying is one of the most frequently cited passages in the whole poem — a handful of lines, disproportionate emotional weight.

landmarks.name: Counting the Suitors in the Hall
landmarks.narrative: More than a hundred men living off another man's house and patience.
landmarks.historicalNote: The scale of the suitors — over a hundred men in most manuscript traditions — already struck ancient commentators as implausibly large for a single household to support.

landmarks.name: The Bow That Only One Man Can String
landmarks.narrative: A contest set for a queen's hand that no suitor can complete.
landmarks.historicalNote: A hero proving himself by alone stringing an unusually stiff bow is a recognized folk-tale motif for establishing a unique right to rule, found well beyond this poem.

landmarks.name: The Hall Barred From the Inside
landmarks.narrative: Doors sealed, weapons gathered, twenty years of debt about to be called in.
landmarks.historicalNote: Just before the killing, the poem has the seer Theoclymenus describe darkness swallowing the sun in daylight — a passage some modern astronomers have linked to a real total solar eclipse over Ithaca around 1178 BCE, though the theory remains debated.

landmarks.name: Ithaca, Truly Home
landmarks.narrative: The last suitor falls, and the house finally belongs to the man who built it.
landmarks.historicalNote: The poem's actual ending, often trimmed from retellings, includes a further peacemaking between Odysseus and the dead suitors' families — present in the original text past the final duel.
